title: Stop Looking for Shortcuts in Education
author: Beanie Geoghegan
summary: Geoghegan argues K-12 education keeps falling for the same cycle: a vendor pitches an "innovative" way to make learning faster or more engaging, weak and interest-funded research is produced, billions are spent, and only afterward do educators see the damage. She traces two rounds of this pattern: the whole-language detour that left a generation with poor literacy foundations, and the one-to-one device wave that has produced students who can't hold pencils, finish books, or write without AI help. The "balance" framing being offered now for screens, she argues, is the same rhetorical move that bought phonics-skeptic curricula another decade of cover. Her counter-claim is that education is the slow, effortful formation of a person through explicit instruction, repetition, and practice, with no fast-track or loophole available. The ask is for leaders at every level (boards, superintendents, principals) to stop chasing edu-fads and invest in refining what has worked for eons.
points: The same pattern repeats: vendor promises, interest-funded "research," billions spent, and teachers absorbing the remediation bill. Pattern recognition is the defense.
Whole-language and one-to-one devices share a structural move: both offered a substitute for the slow work of instruction, and both produced delayed, distributed harm.
"Balance" is a rhetorical escape hatch for failed interventions; the word should trigger scrutiny rather than compromise.
Education is formation, not delivery; it requires explicit instruction, repetition, and patience, and cannot be shortcut by engagement or ease.
The leverage sits with state leaders, school board members, superintendents, and principals, who are the ones typically sold the fad.
quotes: Education is the formation of a human being. It is the slow, sometimes arduous process of leading students to knowledge and helping them make connections with that knowledge. It requires explicit instruction, repetition, and practice.
Education requires time, effort (on the part of teachers and students), and patience. There is no fast-track or loophole.
We keep fighting the same battle in K-12 education decade after decade. Someone comes along with an 'innovative' way to make learning more 'engaging', 'fun', and easier.
Only after pouring billions of dollars into the method, program, or equipment needed do teachers (and sometimes administrators) recognize the problems.
State education leaders, school board members, district superintendents, and school leaders need to quit getting distracted by every shiny new edu-fad that comes along.

Instead of being sucked in by the empty promises of 'quick fixes', we should all be working to understand and refine what has worked in the past so this next generation receives the most excellent education imaginable.

The result: we're now seeing elementary students who can't hold pencils or write their names properly. We have middle and high school students who are unable to read whole books. And college professors are lamenting that their students lack the ability to write essays without the help of AI.” Archived from Beanie's Blog (Substack) on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
